Annotated solutions to problems A, B and C of ABC 156. Source AtCoder Beginner Contest 156

On a contest site, a member's displayed rating equals their inner rating if they have taken part in 10 or more contests. Otherwise, the displayed rating is the inner rating minus 100 × (10 − N), where N is the number of contests. Given N and the displayed rating R, find the inner rating.
#include <stdio.h> int main() { int n, r; scanf("%d %d", &n, &r); if (n >= 10) { printf("%d\n", r); } else { printf("%d\n", r + 100 * (10 - n)); } return 0; }
Just invert the formula: with fewer than 10 contests, the inner rating is R + 100 × (10 − N).
Metric Complexity Time O(1) Space O(1)
Given a positive integer N and a base K, find how many digits N has when written in base K.
#include <stdio.h> int main() { int n, k, digits = 0; scanf("%d %d", &n, &k); while (n > 0) { n /= k; digits++; } printf("%d\n", digits); return 0; }
Each integer division by K removes one base-K digit. The number of divisions until N reaches zero is the digit count.
Metric Complexity Time O(log_K N) Space O(1)

There are N people on a number line, the i-th one at coordinate Xᵢ. A meeting will be held at an integer coordinate P, and the i-th person spends (Xᵢ − P)² stamina to get there. Find the minimum total stamina.

#include <stdio.h> int main() { int n; scanf("%d", &n); int x[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { scanf("%d", &x[i]); } int min = x[0], max = x[0]; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) { if (x[i] < min) min = x[i]; if (x[i] > max) max = x[i]; } int best = -1; for (int p = min; p <= max; p++) { int total = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { total += (x[i] - p) * (x[i] - p); } if (best == -1 || total < best) { best = total; } } printf("%d\n", best); return 0; }

The optimal point always lies between the smallest and largest coordinates, so it is enough to try every integer P in that range and keep the lowest cost. With N ≤ 100 and Xᵢ ≤ 100, brute force is enough.
Metric Complexity Time O(N × (max − min)) Space O(N)

There are three stations, each operated by company A or company B, described by a string S of length 3. A bus line will connect every pair of stations operated by different companies. Determine whether at least one bus line exists.
#include <stdio.h> int main() { char s[4]; scanf("%s", s); if (s[0] != s[1] || s[1] != s[2]) { printf("Yes\n"); } else { printf("No\n"); } return 0; }
A bus line exists whenever the three stations are not all run by the same company, that is, when S has at least two different characters.
Metric Complexity Time O(1) Space O(1)
Balls are placed in a row by repeating the following process: first A blue balls, then B red balls. Find how many blue balls there are among the first N balls in the row.

#include <stdio.h> int main() { long long n, a, b; scanf("%lld %lld %lld", &n, &a, &b); long long cycles = n / (a + b); long long remainder = n % (a + b); long long blue = cycles * a + (remainder < a ? remainder : a); printf("%lld\n", blue); return 0; }

The row repeats in cycles of A + B balls, each with A blue ones. The complete cycles within N contribute (N / (A + B)) × A blue balls. The incomplete cycle contributes min(remainder, A) blue balls, since blue ones come first. Since N, A and B can reach 10¹⁸, long long is required.
Metric Complexity Time O(1) Space O(1)
Annotated solution to problem A of ABC 175. Source AtCoder Beginner Contest 175
Given a string S of length 3, where each character is R (rainy) or S (sunny), find the maximum number of consecutive rainy days.

#include <stdio.h> int main() { char s[4]; scanf("%s", s); int best = 0, current = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { current = (s[i] == 'R') ? current + 1 : 0; if (current > best) best = current; } printf("%d\n", best); return 0; }

Walk through the days keeping the length of the current run of rainy days. On a rainy day, extend the run; on a sunny day, reset it. Keep the largest value the run reached. The same idea works for strings of any length, without enumerating all 8 possible combinations.
Metric Complexity Time O(n) Space O(1)

Rebuilding a binary tree from two traversals, using the fact that preorder reveals the roots and inorder separates the subtrees. Source LeetCode 105 — Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
documents.s: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal

documents.t: Given two integer arrays preorder and inorder, which are, respectively, the preorder and inorder traversals of the same binary tree (with distinct values), construct and return the tree.

class TreeNode { val: number; left: TreeNode | null; right: TreeNode | null; constructor(val?: number, left?: TreeNode | null, right?: TreeNode | null) { this.val = val ?? 0; this.left = left ?? null; this.right = right ?? null; } } function buildTree(preorder: number[], inorder: number[]): TreeNode | null { if (!inorder.length) { return null; } const index = inorder.indexOf(preorder.shift()!); const root = new TreeNode(inorder[index]); root.left = buildTree(preorder, inorder.slice(0, index)); root.right = buildTree(preorder, inorder.slice(index + 1)); return root; }

The first element of preorder is always the root of the current (sub)tree. Locate that root in inorder: everything to its left belongs to the left subtree and everything to its right to the right subtree. Repeat the process recursively for each side. Since preorder visits the left subtree before the right one, consuming preorder with shift() yields the roots in the right order.

Metric Complexity Time O(n²) Space O(n²) In the worst case (a degenerate tree), each call performs indexOf, shift and slice in O(n), and the copies of inorder add up to O(n²) memory. Optimization Precomputing a value → index Map for inorder, walking preorder with an index and working with bounds (left, right) instead of slice brings both time and space down to O(n).

function levelOrder(root: TreeNode | null): (number | null)[] { const result: (number | null)[] = []; const queue = [root]; while (queue.length) { const node = queue.shift()!; result.push(node ? node.val : null); if (node) queue.push(node.left, node.right); } while (result.at(-1) === null) result.pop(); return result; } console.log(levelOrder(buildTree([3, 9, 20, 15, 7], [9, 3, 15, 20, 7]))); // Output: [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] console.log(levelOrder(buildTree([-1], [-1]))); // Output: [-1]
Converting a Roman numeral to an integer by walking the string once and handling the subtraction cases. Source LeetCode 13 — Roman to Integer

Given a string s holding a valid Roman numeral, return the corresponding integer. The symbols and their values are: Symbol Value I 1 V 5 X 10 L 50 C 100 D 500 M 1000 A smaller symbol before a larger one means subtraction, only in these cases: I before V and X: 4 and 9 X before L and C: 40 and 90 C before D and M: 400 and 900

const VALUES: Record<string, number> = { I: 1, V: 5, X: 10, L: 50, C: 100, D: 500, M: 1000, }; function romanToInt(s: string): number { let result = 0; for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) { const current = VALUES[s[i]]; const next = i + 1 < s.length ? VALUES[s[i + 1]] : 0; if (current < next) { result += next - current; i++; // the next symbol has already been consumed } else { result += current; } } return result; }

Walk through the string comparing each symbol with the next one. If the current one is smaller than the next, add their difference (subtraction case, such as IV = 4) and skip the next one. Otherwise, add only the current symbol's value.
Metric Complexity Time O(n) Space O(1)

console.log(romanToInt("III")); // Output: 3 console.log(romanToInt("IV")); // Output: 4 console.log(romanToInt("IX")); // Output: 9 console.log(romanToInt("XL")); // Output: 40 console.log(romanToInt("CM")); // Output: 900 console.log(romanToInt("LVIII")); // Output: 58 console.log(romanToInt("MCMXCIV")); // Output: 1994
Finding the only unpaired element of an array, in linear time and constant memory, using the XOR operator. Source LeetCode 136 — Single Number
Given a non-empty array of integers nums where every element appears twice except one, find that element. The solution must run in O(n) time and use only O(1) extra space.
function singleNumber(nums: number[]): number { let result = 0; for (const num of nums) { result ^= num; } return result; }

The solution relies on three properties of XOR (^): Self-inverse: x ^ x = 0 Identity: x ^ 0 = x Commutativity and associativity: the order of operations does not change the result XOR-ing every element cancels out each pair, leaving only the number that appears once.
Metric Complexity Time O(n) Space O(1)

console.log(singleNumber([2, 2, 1])); // Output: 1 console.log(singleNumber([4, 1, 2, 1, 2])); // Output: 4 console.log(singleNumber([1])); // Output: 1 console.log(singleNumber([-1, -1, -2])); // Output: -2
Sorting a linked list in O(n log n) by adapting Merge Sort, which only needs to adjust pointers. Source LeetCode 148 — Sort List
Given the head of a linked list, return the list sorted in ascending order.

class ListNode { val: number; next: ListNode | null; constructor(val?: number, next?: ListNode | null) { this.val = val ?? 0; this.next = next ?? null; } } function sortList(head: ListNode | null): ListNode | null { if (!head || !head.next) { return head; } // Find the middle with slow and fast pointers let slow = head; let fast = head.next; while (fast && fast.next) { slow = slow.next!; fast = fast.next.next; } // Split the list into two halves const mid = slow.next; slow.next = null; return merge(sortList(head), sortList(mid)); } function merge(l1: ListNode | null, l2: ListNode | null): ListNode | null { const dummy = new ListNode(); let current = dummy; while (l1 && l2) { if (l1.val <= l2.val) { current.next = l1; l1 = l1.next; } else { current.next = l2; l2 = l2.next; } current = current.next; } current.next = l1 ?? l2; return dummy.next; }

Find the middle of the list with two pointers: the slow one moves one node at a time and the fast one, two. When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow one is at the middle. Cut the list into two halves. Sort each half recursively. Merge the two sorted halves, using a sentinel node (dummy) to simplify building the resulting list.
Metric Complexity Time O(n log n) Space O(log n) The space comes from the recursion stack; merging allocates no new nodes. The solution is stable.

function fromArray(values: number[]): ListNode | null { return values.reduceRight<ListNode | null>((next, val) => new ListNode(val, next), null); } function toArray(head: ListNode | null): number[] { const values: number[] = []; for (let node = head; node; node = node.next) values.push(node.val); return values; } console.log(toArray(sortList(fromArray([4, 2, 1, 3])))); // Output: [1, 2, 3, 4] console.log(toArray(sortList(fromArray([-1, 5, 3, 4, 0])))); // Output: [-1, 0, 3, 4, 5] console.log(toArray(sortList(fromArray([3, 1, 3, 1])))); // Output: [1, 1, 3, 3] console.log(toArray(sortList(fromArray([])))); // Output: []
Finding two elements of an array that add up to a target value, using a hash map to solve it in a single pass. Source LeetCode 1 — Two Sum

Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers in nums that add up to target. Each input has exactly one solution, and the same element may not be used twice.

function twoSum(nums: number[], target: number): number[] { const seen = new Map<number, number>(); // value -> index for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) { const complement = target - nums[i]; if (seen.has(complement)) { return [seen.get(complement)!, i]; } seen.set(nums[i], i); } return []; }

For each number, compute the complement still needed to reach the target (target - nums[i]). If the complement has already been seen, the two indices are the answer. Otherwise, store the current number and its index in the hash map. Brute force compares every pair in O(n²); the hash map trades that cost for O(n) memory.
Metric Complexity Time O(n) Space O(n)
console.log(twoSum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9)); // Output: [0, 1] console.log(twoSum([-1, -2, -3, -4, -5], -8)); // Output: [2, 4] console.log(twoSum([3, 3], 6)); // Output: [0, 1]

Breadth-first search (BFS) traverses a graph by visiting all the neighbors of a vertex before moving on to the next level. That is why it finds the shortest path in number of edges in unweighted graphs.

Mark the source vertex as visited and put it in a queue. While the queue is not empty, take the vertex at the front. For each neighbor not yet visited, mark it as visited and add it to the back of the queue. Since the queue is FIFO, every vertex at distance k is processed before any vertex at distance k + 1.
Metric Complexity Time O(V + E) Space O(V) V is the number of vertices and E the number of edges. Each vertex enters the queue once and each edge is examined once (twice, in undirected graphs).

from collections import deque def bfs(graph, start): visited = {start} queue = deque([start]) order = [] while queue: node = queue.popleft() order.append(node) for neighbor in graph[node]: if neighbor not in visited: visited.add(neighbor) queue.append(neighbor) return order
Finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs Explores the graph predictably, level by level
Can use a lot of memory on wide graphs, since the queue holds an entire level Ignores edge weights
To get the fewest steps between two vertices To explore every vertex of a level before going deeper (social networks, web crawlers, mazes)
Queue FIFO Depth-first search (DFS) Dijkstra's algorithm (shortest paths in weighted graphs)
A greedy algorithm makes, at each step, the choice that looks best at that moment, without reconsidering it later, hoping to reach a globally optimal solution.

Define a selection criterion (for example, "the most valuable item" or "the activity that ends earliest"). Sort or prioritize the candidates by that criterion. Walk through the candidates, accepting each one that keeps the solution feasible. The strategy only guarantees the optimum when the problem has two properties: Greedy choice: there is an optimal solution that starts with the locally optimal choice Optimal substructure: the optimal solution contains optimal solutions to its subproblems def greedy(items, criteria, is_feasible): result = [] for item in sorted(items, key=criteria): if is_feasible(result, item): result.append(item) return result
Metric Complexity Time O(n log n) (typical) Space O(n) The cost is usually dominated by the initial sort; the selection itself is O(n).

Making change with the fewest coins: def make_change(amount, coins): """Works for canonical coin systems, such as 25, 10, 5 and 1.""" result = [] for coin in sorted(coins, reverse=True): while amount >= coin: result.append(coin) amount -= coin return result print(make_change(67, [25, 10, 5, 1])) # Output: [25, 25, 10, 5, 1, 1] Not always optimal With coins [4, 3, 1] and amount 6, the greedy strategy returns [4, 1, 1] (3 coins), but the optimum is [3, 3] (2 coins). In such cases, use dynamic programming.
Paradigm Characteristic Greedy Local, irreversible choices Dynamic programming Considers every subproblem and memoizes Backtracking Explores solutions and backtracks as needed

Activity selection: always pick the activity that ends earliest Huffman coding: shorter codes for the most frequent symbols Fractional knapsack: take items in decreasing order of value per weight Minimum spanning tree: Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms Shortest path: Dijkstra's algorithm
Simple to implement Efficient, usually O(n log n) Low memory usage
Does not always find the global optimum Requires a proof that the greedy choice is correct
When you can prove the local choice leads to the global optimum When a fast approximate solution is good enough
Big O notation Quick Sort Dynamic programming

Binary search finds an element in a sorted array by halving the search interval at each step, until it finds the target or the interval is exhausted. Prerequisite The array must be sorted. On an unsorted array, binary search may miss elements that are present.

Compare the middle element of the interval with the target. If they are equal, return the middle position. If the target is smaller, keep searching only the left half. If the target is larger, keep searching only the right half. Repeat until the target is found or the interval is empty.
Metric Complexity Time (best case) O(1) Time (average case) O(log n) Time (worst case) O(log n) Space O(1) iterative, O(log n) recursive

def binary_search(arr, target): left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1 while left <= right: mid = (left + right) // 2 if arr[mid] == target: return mid if arr[mid] < target: left = mid + 1 else: right = mid - 1 return -1 # not found

def binary_search_recursive(arr, target, left=0, right=None): if right is None: right = len(arr) - 1 if left > right: return -1 mid = (left + right) // 2 if arr[mid] == target: return mid if arr[mid] < target: return binary_search_recursive(arr, target, mid + 1, right) return binary_search_recursive(arr, target, left, mid - 1)
Very efficient on large arrays The iterative version uses no extra memory
Requires sorted data Requires O(1) access by index, which does not work well on linked lists The recursive version uses O(log n) stack space
For repeated searches over a large sorted collection To find boundaries in monotonic search spaces (for example, the smallest value that satisfies a condition)
Array Big O notation Binary tree

Bubble Sort is a comparison-based sorting algorithm that walks through the array several times, swapping adjacent pairs that are out of order. On each pass, the largest remaining element "bubbles up" to the end.

Walk through the array comparing each pair of adjacent elements. If the current element is greater than the next one, swap them. At the end of the pass, the largest element is in the last position of the unsorted part. Repeat, skipping the sorted part, until a pass finishes with no swaps.

Metric Complexity Time (best case) O(n) Time (average case) O(n²) Time (worst case) O(n²) Space O(1) The best case happens with an already sorted array, thanks to the early exit when no swaps occur. The algorithm is stable and in-place.
def bubble_sort(arr): n = len(arr) for i in range(n): swapped = False for j in range(n - i - 1): if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]: arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j] swapped = True if not swapped: break
Simple to understand and implement Uses no extra memory Detects an already sorted array in O(n)
Very slow for large arrays Rarely used outside teaching contexts
To learn the fundamentals of sorting On very small or nearly sorted collections
Selection Sort Merge Sort Swap Insertion Sort
Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm: it splits the array into two halves, sorts each one recursively and then merges the two sorted halves.

If the array has 0 or 1 elements, it is already sorted. Split the array into two halves. Sort each half recursively. Merge the two halves by comparing their first elements and always copying the smaller one.
Metric Complexity Time O(n log n) Space O(n) The array is split log n times, and each recursion level does O(n) work while merging. The algorithm is stable but not in-place.

function mergeSort(arr: number[]): number[] { if (arr.length <= 1) { return arr; } const mid = Math.floor(arr.length / 2); const left = arr.slice(0, mid); const right = arr.slice(mid); return merge(mergeSort(left), mergeSort(right)); } function merge(left: number[], right: number[]): number[] { const result: number[] = []; let i = 0; let j = 0; while (i < left.length && j < right.length) { // <= keeps the relative order of equal elements (stability) if (left[i] <= right[j]) { result.push(left[i++]); } else { result.push(right[j++]); } } return result.concat(left.slice(i), right.slice(j)); }
Guaranteed O(n log n) in every case Stable Great for linked lists and for sorting data that does not fit in memory (external sorting)
Uses O(n) extra memory Slower than simple algorithms on small arrays
When the sort must be stable When worst-case performance matters To sort linked lists
Quick Sort Sort List Big O notation

Quick Sort is a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that picks an element as the pivot and partitions the array around it: smaller elements to the left, larger ones to the right. It then sorts each side recursively.

Pick a pivot (in this implementation, the last element). Partition the array so that elements less than or equal to the pivot end up on the left and larger ones on the right. Place the pivot between the two parts, in its final position. Apply the same process recursively to the left and right parts.

Metric Complexity Time (best case) O(n log n) Time (average case) O(n log n) Time (worst case) O(n²) Space O(log n) The worst case happens when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element (for example, using the last element as pivot on an already sorted array). The algorithm is in-place but not stable.

function quickSort(arr: number[], low = 0, high = arr.length - 1): number[] { if (low < high) { const pivotIndex = partition(arr, low, high); quickSort(arr, low, pivotIndex - 1); quickSort(arr, pivotIndex + 1, high); } return arr; } function partition(arr: number[], low: number, high: number): number { const pivot = arr[high]; let i = low - 1; for (let j = low; j < high; j++) { if (arr[j] <= pivot) { i++; [arr[i], arr[j]] = [arr[j], arr[i]]; } } // Place the pivot in its final position [arr[i + 1], arr[high]] = [arr[high], arr[i + 1]]; return i + 1; }
Very fast in practice, with low constants In-place, uses little memory Good cache usage

O(n²) in the worst case Not stable Performance depends on the pivot choice Avoiding the worst case Choosing the pivot at random, or as the median of three elements (start, middle and end), makes the worst case very unlikely.
To sort large in-memory arrays When extra memory is a constraint When stability is not required
Selection Sort is a comparison-based sorting algorithm that, on each pass, selects the smallest element of the unsorted part and puts it in its final position.

Find the smallest element in the unsorted part of the array. Swap it with the first element of the unsorted part. Move the boundary of the sorted part one position forward. Repeat until the whole array is sorted.
Metric Complexity Time O(n²) Space O(1) The number of comparisons is always the same regardless of the input, so all three cases are O(n²). The algorithm is in-place but not stable.
def selection_sort(arr): n = len(arr) for i in range(n): min_idx = i for j in range(i + 1, n): if arr[j] < arr[min_idx]: min_idx = j arr[i], arr[min_idx] = arr[min_idx], arr[i]
Simple to understand and implement Uses no extra memory Performs at most n − 1 swaps, useful when writing to memory is expensive
Very slow for large arrays Does not benefit from nearly sorted arrays Not stable
For teaching, when comparing sorting algorithms On very small collections, where simplicity matters more than performance
Bubble Sort Quick Sort Swap Insertion Sort
The principles that show up in almost every algorithm and system: how to measure efficiency, how memory is organized, how data enters and leaves a collection, and how tasks run in parallel.

Topic Summary Big O Notation How time and memory grow as the input increases Stack and Heap The two main memory regions of a program FIFO First in, first out LIFO Last in, first out Swap Exchanging values between variables or positions Threads Concurrent execution inside a process Serverless Cloud computing without managing servers Where to start Start with Big O Notation: it is the language used throughout the rest of the site to compare data structures and algorithms.
Big O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory usage grows as the input size (n) increases. It does not measure real time in seconds, but the growth rate in the worst case.

Count the operations performed as a function of n. Keep only the fastest-growing term. Drop multiplicative constants. For example, an algorithm that performs 3n² + 5n + 2 operations is O(n²): for large inputs, the n² term dominates the others. def has_duplicates(items): for i in range(len(items)): # n iterations for j in range(i + 1, len(items)): # up to n iterations if items[i] == items[j]: return True return False # Two nested loops over n elements: O(n²)

Complexity Name Growth Example O(1) Constant Does not depend on n Accessing an array by index O(log n) Logarithmic Halves the problem Binary search O(n) Linear Proportional to n Iterating over a list O(n log n) Quasilinear Between linear and quadratic Merge Sort, Quick Sort (average) O(n²) Quadratic Compares every pair Bubble Sort, Selection Sort O(2ⁿ) Exponential Doubles with each new element Generating every subset O(n!) Factorial Tries every permutation Brute-force traveling salesman From most to least efficient: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!) O(2ⁿ) and O(n!) become impractical even for small inputs: with n = 20, O(2ⁿ) already exceeds one million operations and O(n!) exceeds 10¹⁸.
Comparing solutions before implementing them Choosing the right data structure for each operation Predicting whether an algorithm will scale to large inputs

When deciding between two approaches to the same problem When checking whether a solution fits a contest problem's time limits How to remember O(1): direct access · O(log n): halving · O(n): one loop · O(n log n): divide and conquer · O(n²): two nested loops · O(2ⁿ): every combination · O(n!): every ordering
Binary search Merge Sort Data structures
FIFO ("first in, first out") is the policy in which elements are removed in the same order they were added, like a supermarket checkout line: whoever arrives first is served first.
The structure that implements FIFO is the queue, with two operations: Enqueue: adds an element to the back Dequeue: removes the element at the front
Operation Complexity Enqueue O(1) Dequeue O(1)

from collections import deque class Queue: def __init__(self): self.items = deque() def enqueue(self, item): self.items.append(item) def dequeue(self): return self.items.popleft() if self.items else None def is_empty(self): return len(self.items) == 0 queue = Queue() queue.enqueue(1) queue.enqueue(2) queue.enqueue(3) print(queue.dequeue()) # Output: 1 print(queue.dequeue()) # Output: 2 Watch out for lists In Python, list.pop(0) is O(n) because it shifts every element. Use collections.deque to get O(1) at both ends.
Print and task queues Process scheduling Network and I/O buffers Breadth-first search (BFS)
LIFO ("last in, first out") is the policy in which the element removed is always the most recent one, like a stack of plates: the last one placed on top is the first one taken off.
The structure that implements LIFO is the stack. Insertions and removals happen at a single end, the top: Push: adds an element to the top Pop: removes the element from the top
Operation Complexity Push O(1) Pop O(1)

class Stack: def __init__(self): self.items = [] def push(self, item): self.items.append(item) def pop(self): return self.items.pop() if self.items else None def is_empty(self): return len(self.items) == 0 stack = Stack() stack.push(1) stack.push(2) stack.push(3) print(stack.pop()) # Output: 3 print(stack.pop()) # Output: 2
Function call stack Undo/redo in editors Expression evaluation and bracket matching Depth-first search (DFS)
FIFO Stack Stack and heap memory
While running, a program uses two main memory regions: the stack, for temporary data from function calls, and the heap, for dynamically allocated data that must outlive a single call.

Each function call pushes a block (frame) onto the stack containing: Function parameters Local variables (especially primitive types) Return address When the function returns, the frame is removed automatically. The stack follows the LIFO model: the last frame pushed is the first one removed. Allocation: automatic, managed by the runtime Speed: very fast Size: limited; deep recursion causes a stack overflow

The heap holds memory reserved on demand at run time, such as objects, lists, trees and graphs. Allocation: manual in C/C++ (malloc/free), automatic via a garbage collector in Java, JavaScript, Python and C# Speed: slower than the stack, due to management overhead Size: usually much larger than the stack Risks: memory leaks in languages without a garbage collector def build_list(n): size = n # 'size' and the 'items' reference live in the frame (stack) items = [0] * size # the list itself is allocated on the heap return items # the frame is discarded; the list stays on the heap

Characteristic Stack Heap Allocation Automatic Manual (C/C++) or automatic (GC) Speed Very fast Slower Size Limited Usually larger Usage Local variables and calls Objects and dynamic structures Deallocation When the function returns Manual or by the garbage collector Risks Stack overflow Leaks and fragmentation
Stack: small data whose lifetime is limited to one function Heap: large data, data whose size is unknown at compile time, or data that must outlive the function that created it

Serverless is a cloud computing model in which the provider manages all of the infrastructure. Instead of maintaining servers, you publish functions that run on demand, in response to events such as HTTP requests or file uploads.

Write a function with the business logic. Attach the function to a trigger (HTTP request, queue message, uploaded file). On each event, the provider creates or reuses an environment, runs the function and bills for the execution time. No server management: provisioning, patching and availability are handled by the provider (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions) Automatic scaling: the number of executions follows demand Pay per use: no cost for idle servers

An AWS Lambda function in Python that answers an HTTP request: import json def handler(event, context): name = (event.get("queryStringParameters") or {}).get("name", "world") return { "statusCode": 200, "body": json.dumps({"message": f"Hello, {name}!"}), }
REST APIs File processing (images, videos) Scheduled task automation Event-driven system integration
Lower operational costs Faster development, focused on business logic Scalability and high availability with no configuration
Limits on execution time and resources Cold start: extra latency on the first run after an idle period Vendor lock-in Harder debugging and monitoring
Intermittent or unpredictable workloads Short, event-triggered tasks Prototypes and early-stage products

Swap is the operation of exchanging the values of two variables (or two array positions): after the swap, each one holds the value the other had. It is the foundation of sorting algorithms such as Bubble Sort, Selection Sort and Quick Sort.
The classic approach uses a third variable so that neither value is lost during the swap. a, b = 5, 10 temp = a a = b b = temp print(a, b) # Output: 10 5
Many languages swap values directly through multiple assignment (or destructuring), without an explicit temporary variable. a, b = b, a [a, b] = [b, a];
Metric Complexity Time O(1) Space O(1)

Reversing an array with two indices that walk from both ends toward the center, swapping each pair of elements: function reverse(array: number[]): number[] { let left = 0; let right = array.length - 1; while (left < right) { [array[left], array[right]] = [array[right], array[left]]; left++; right--; } return array; } console.log(reverse([10, 30, 40, 55])); // Output: [55, 40, 30, 10]
Comparison-based sorting algorithms Reversing and rotating arrays Shuffling (Fisher–Yates algorithm)
Bubble Sort Selection Sort Quick Sort
A thread is the smallest unit of execution the operating system can schedule. A process can have several threads running concurrently, all sharing the same memory space.

Each thread has its own call stack and registers All threads in a process share the heap, the code and open files The operating system switches between threads (or runs them in parallel on different cores) Sharing memory makes communication between threads cheap, but requires synchronization (locks, semaphores, queues) to avoid race conditions, where the result depends on the order of execution.

Downloading a file and processing data at the same time instead of sequentially: import threading import time def download_file(): print("Downloading file...") time.sleep(5) # simulates the download print("File downloaded") def process_data(): print("Processing data...") time.sleep(3) # simulates the processing print("Data processed") download = threading.Thread(target=download_file) process = threading.Thread(target=process_data) download.start() process.start() download.join() # wait for both threads to finish process.join() print("Tasks finished") # after ~5 s, not 8 s Python's GIL In CPython, the Global Interpreter Lock prevents two threads from running Python bytecode at the same time. Threads still help with I/O-bound work (network, disk); for CPU-bound work, use multiprocessing.
Makes use of idle time during I/O operations Cheap communication through shared memory Lighter to create than processes
Race conditions and deadlocks Hard to debug, since bugs depend on execution order A failure in one thread can bring down the whole process
When the program spends a lot of time waiting on I/O (network requests, file reads) When the interface must stay responsive during a long task

A data structure defines how data is organized and, as a result, how much it costs to access, insert, search or remove an element. Choosing the right structure often matters more than optimizing the code itself.

Structure Access Search Insertion Removal Array O(1) O(n) O(n) O(n) Linked List O(n) O(n) O(1) at head O(1) at head Stack O(1) top O(n) O(1) O(1) Queue O(1) front O(n) O(1) O(1) Binary Search Tree O(log n)* O(log n)* O(log n)* O(log n)* * For balanced trees. In the worst case (a degenerate tree), operations degrade to O(n). Where to start If you are not yet familiar with Big O Notation, read it first: the table above uses it.
An array stores a sequence of elements of the same type in contiguous memory positions. Since each element's position can be computed from its index, access is immediate.

Indexed: element i lives at address start + i × element_size Fixed size: set at creation, in most low-level languages Homogeneous: every element has the same type Dynamic arrays (list in Python, vector in C++, Array in JavaScript) double their capacity when full, which makes appending O(1) amortized.
Operation Complexity Access by index O(1) Update by index O(1) Search by value O(n) Append O(1) amortized Insert/remove in the middle O(n)

arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] print(arr[2]) # Output: 30 arr[1] = 25 print(arr) # Output: [10, 25, 30, 40, 50] if 40 in arr: # linear search print("Found") arr.append(60) # insert at the end arr.remove(30) # remove by value, shifting the following elements print(arr) # Output: [10, 25, 40, 50, 60]
Collections with frequent access by position Building block for other structures (stacks, queues, heaps, hash tables) Matrices and buffers
O(1) access by index Excellent cache usage, thanks to contiguous memory No extra memory overhead per element
Fixed size for static arrays Insertions and removals in the middle cost O(n) Every element must have the same type (in typed languages)
When the number of elements is known or rarely changes When access by index is the most frequent operation

A binary tree is a hierarchical structure in which each node has at most two children, called the left child and the right child. When the values follow the rule left < node < right, it is a binary search tree (BST).

Root: the node at the top of the tree Leaf: a node with no children Height: length of the longest path from the root to a leaf Depth: length of the path from the root to a node Common types: Full: every node has 0 or 2 children Complete: every level is full except possibly the last, filled from left to right Perfect: every internal node has two children and every leaf is on the same level Balanced: the height is kept at O(log n)

For a binary search tree: Operation Complexity (balanced) Complexity (worst case) Search O(log n) O(n) Insert O(log n) O(n) Remove O(log n) O(n) Traversal O(n) O(n) The worst case happens when the tree degenerates into a list, for example when inserting already sorted values.

class Node: def __init__(self, data): self.data = data self.left = None self.right = None def inorder(root): """In-order traversal: left, node, right.""" if root: inorder(root.left) print(root.data, end=" ") inorder(root.right) root = Node(10) root.left = Node(5) root.right = Node(15) root.left.left = Node(2) root.left.right = Node(7) inorder(root) # Output: 2 5 7 10 15
Hierarchical data (file systems, org charts) Expression trees in compilers Search trees for fast search, insertion and removal Heaps for priority queues
O(log n) operations when balanced In-order traversal returns values in sorted order (BST)
Can become unbalanced and degrade to O(n) More complex to implement than arrays and lists
To represent hierarchical relationships When search, insertion and removal must be efficient and the data must stay sorted
Construct Binary Tree Binary search AVL and red-black trees (self-balancing search trees)
A linked list is a linear structure made of nodes, where each node stores a value and a reference to the next one. Unlike an array, nodes do not need to sit in contiguous memory.

Singly linked list: each node points to the next one Doubly linked list: each node points to the next and the previous one Circular list: the last node points back to the first one The list keeps a reference to the first node, the head. To reach any other node, you must traverse the list from it.
Operation Complexity Access by position O(n) Search by value O(n) Insert/remove at the head O(1) Insert/remove after a known node O(1) Append (without a tail pointer) O(n)

class Node: def __init__(self, data): self.data = data self.next = None class LinkedList: def __init__(self): self.head = None def prepend(self, data): node = Node(data) node.next = self.head self.head = node def append(self, data): node = Node(data) if not self.head: self.head = node return last = self.head while last.next: last = last.next last.next = node def __str__(self): values, current = [], self.head while current: values.append(str(current.data)) current = current.next return " -> ".join(values) linked = LinkedList() linked.append(20) linked.append(30) linked.prepend(10) print(linked) # Output: 10 -> 20 -> 30
Implementing stacks, queues and deques Adjacency lists in graphs Undo/redo history LRU caches (doubly linked list + hash table)
O(1) insertion and removal at known positions Grows and shrinks without reallocation
No direct access by index Extra memory for pointers Worse cache usage than arrays
When there are many insertions and removals at the start or in the middle When the collection size changes often
A queue is a linear structure that follows the FIFO policy: the first element inserted is the first one removed. Elements enter at the back and leave from the front.
Enqueue: adds an element to the back Dequeue: removes and returns the front element Peek: reads the front without removing it Is empty: checks whether the queue is empty
Operation Complexity Enqueue O(1) Dequeue O(1) Peek O(1) Search O(n)

In Python, collections.deque provides O(1) at both ends: from collections import deque queue = deque() queue.append(10) # enqueue queue.append(20) queue.append(30) print(queue[0]) # Output: 10 (peek) print(queue.popleft()) # Output: 10 print(queue.popleft()) # Output: 20 if not queue: print("Queue is empty")
Task scheduling (print queue, CPU) Breadth-first search (BFS) Request handling in servers Data buffers
Every main operation is O(1) Preserves arrival order
Only the front and back are accessible Not suited for random access
When items must be processed in arrival order In algorithms that explore data level by level, such as BFS
A stack is a linear structure that follows the LIFO policy: the last element inserted is the first one removed. Every operation happens at a single end, the top.
Push: adds an element to the top Pop: removes and returns the top element Peek: reads the top without removing it Is empty: checks whether the stack is empty
Operation Complexity Push O(1) Pop O(1) Peek O(1) Search O(n)

In Python, a list already works as a stack by using its end as the top: stack = [] stack.append(10) # push stack.append(20) stack.append(30) print(stack[-1]) # Output: 30 (peek) print(stack.pop()) # Output: 30 print(stack.pop()) # Output: 20 if not stack: print("Stack is empty")
Function call stack Undo/redo in editors Expression evaluation (postfix notation) and bracket matching Parsing and depth-first search (DFS)
Every main operation is O(1) Simple to implement on top of an array or linked list
Only the top is accessible Not suited for random access
When you need to reverse the order of data To keep track of nested or recursive operations
LIFO Queue Stack and heap memory

AWS is Amazon's cloud computing platform, launched in 2006 and a pioneer of the model. It provides on-demand, pay-as-you-go services for compute, storage, databases, networking, artificial intelligence, IoT and security, among others.

Service Category Description EC2 Compute On-demand virtual servers Lambda Compute Serverless function execution S3 Storage Scalable object storage RDS Database Managed relational databases VPC Network Isolated virtual network in the cloud CloudFront Network Content delivery network (CDN) IAM Security Identity and access control

Elasticity: resources scale up and down with demand Pay per use: no upfront hardware investment Global reach: infrastructure spread across regions and availability zones Breadth: hundreds of managed services, from virtual machines to machine learning Today AWS is the global leader in cloud computing, serving everyone from startups to governments and academic institutions.
Regions and AZs IAM Policies Serverless
IAM is the AWS service that controls who can access which resources and what they can do with them. It is a global, free service available in every AWS account.

Every request to AWS is made by an authenticated identity. IAM evaluates the policies attached to that identity and to the resource to decide whether the action is allowed. By default, everything is denied.

Users: people or applications with long-term credentials (password, access keys) Groups: collections of users that share the same permissions Roles: identities with temporary permissions, assumed by users, services or external accounts Policies: JSON documents that define permissions Identity providers: integration with external logins (SAML, OIDC, corporate directories)

Giving each team member only the access they need Letting one service (such as a Lambda function) access another (such as an S3 bucket) without hard-coded keys Granting temporary access to another AWS account Requiring multi-factor authentication (MFA) for sensitive operations

Do not use the root user for everyday tasks Enable MFA, especially for privileged users Grant the minimum permissions required (principle of least privilege) Prefer roles with temporary credentials over long-term access keys Review permissions regularly and remove what is unused

A policy is a JSON document that defines permissions in AWS: who can perform which actions, on which resources and under which conditions. Policies are attached to IAM identities or directly to resources.

Every request starts out denied by default. AWS evaluates every policy that applies to the identity and the resource. If any policy has an explicit Deny for the action, it is denied. Otherwise, if any policy has an Allow, it is allowed.

AWS managed: created and maintained by AWS for common cases (for example, ReadOnlyAccess) Customer managed: created by you and reusable across users, groups and roles Inline: embedded in a single identity, not reusable Resource-based: attached to the resource itself, such as an S3 bucket policy

Version: policy language version (always use 2012-10-17) Statement: list of rules, each with: Effect: Allow or Deny Action: actions allowed or denied (for example, s3:ListBucket) Resource: ARN of the affected resources Condition (optional): extra conditions, such as source IP or MFA usage { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:ListBucket", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket" } ] }

Grant only the permissions required (principle of least privilege) Prefer managed policies over inline ones, for easier maintenance Avoid wildcards ("Action": "*", "Resource": "*") outside test environments Use Condition to restrict access further Validate policies with IAM Access Analyzer

AWS global infrastructure is organized into regions, geographic areas isolated from one another, and each region is made of several availability zones (AZs), groups of physically separate data centers.

Isolation: regions do not share resources by default, which improves security and independence Identification: each region has a code, such as us-east-1 (Northern Virginia) or sa-east-1 (São Paulo) Scope: most services are regional; a few, such as IAM, are global

Composition: one or more independent data centers, with redundant power, networking and connectivity Connection: the AZs of a region are linked by high-speed, low-latency connections Purpose: spreading an application across AZs keeps it running if a data center fails
Physical facilities that house servers, storage and networking equipment. AWS spreads them around the world to ensure availability, redundancy and proximity to end users.

Latency: regions close to users respond faster Cost: prices vary between regions, due to taxes, operating costs and demand Compliance: data protection laws may require data to stay in a given country Service availability: not every service exists in every region

Spread critical applications across at least two AZs Choose the region based on latency, cost and legal requirements Use multiple regions only when there is a real need for disaster recovery or global reach

A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software that creates, manages and manipulates databases, acting as the interface between data, users and applications. An RDBMS is a DBMS based on the relational model, in which data lives in tables related to one another.

Storage: organizes data on disk and in memory Query and manipulation: lets you insert, read, update and delete data Security: controls who can access what Integrity: ensures data follows the defined rules Transactions: groups operations that must all happen or none at all Backup and recovery: protects against data loss
MySQL PostgreSQL Oracle Database Microsoft SQL Server MongoDB (non-relational)

Tables: data organized into rows (records) and columns (attributes) SQL: the standard language to define, query and manipulate data Referential integrity: relationships enforced by primary and foreign keys ACID transactions: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability
MySQL PostgreSQL Oracle Database Microsoft SQL Server SQLite

Characteristic DBMS RDBMS Model Any (document, key-value...) Relational (tables) Language Depends on the system SQL Relationships Not always supported Primary and foreign keys Example MongoDB PostgreSQL Every RDBMS is a DBMS, but not every DBMS is relational.

A relational database stores data in tables that relate to one another through keys. The relational model was proposed by Edgar F. Codd in 1970 and is still the most widely used, thanks to its flexibility, integrity and ease of querying.

Database: an organized set of tables, managed by an RDBMS such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle or SQL Server Table: represents an entity (for example, customers or orders) Column (attribute): a property of the entity, with a name and a data type (integer, text, date) Row (record): one occurrence of the entity, with a value for each column Primary key: column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each row Foreign key: column that references another table's primary key, creating a relationship

A customers table and an orders table, related by the customer_id column: id (PK) name email 1 John Smith john@email.com 2 Mary Jones mary@email.com id (PK) customer_id (FK) total 10 1 150.00 11 1 89.90 12 2 42.00 Each order points to an existing customer; the RDBMS prevents, for example, an order with customer_id = 3 if that customer does not exist.
One to one: each row in A matches at most one row in B One to many: a customer has many orders (the example above) Many to many: students and courses, represented by a junction table

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language to define, query and manipulate data in relational databases. It is declarative: you describe what you want, and the database decides how to execute it.

Category Meaning Commands DDL Data definition CREATE, ALTER, DROP DML Data manipulation INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE DQL Data query SELECT DCL Access control GRANT, REVOKE TCL Transaction control BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK

-- DDL: create the table CREATE TABLE customers ( id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE ); -- DML: insert and update data INSERT INTO customers (id, name, email) VALUES (1, 'John Smith', 'john@email.com'); UPDATE customers SET name = 'John P. Smith' WHERE id = 1; -- DQL: query data SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE email LIKE '%@email.com' ORDER BY name; -- DML: delete data DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1;
Creating and changing the database structure (tables, indexes, views) Inserting, updating and deleting records Querying and combining data from several tables (JOIN) Controlling access permissions

Always use WHERE in UPDATE and DELETE, and check the filter with a SELECT first List columns instead of using SELECT * in production code Use parameters (prepared statements) instead of concatenating values, to avoid SQL injection Index columns frequently used in filters and JOINs
